suggestions.direction: Recast messages as claims that buyers and sellers interpret, and theorize which rhetorical content builds legitimacy, trust or relational framing in an exchange that would otherwise be purely transactional (for example, justifications, appeals to fairness, identity cues). Code the messages for these constructs before testing them.
suggestions.why: The journal values theories of how audiences make meaning from signals, more than estimates of whether communication reduces breakdown.

suggestions.direction: Build the experience result into a theory of organizational and vicarious learning. Test whether sellers learn from their own feedback (acceptances and rejections) or by imitating the norms of experienced sellers, and whether this narrows the variety of messages over time.
suggestions.why: Linking learning to exploration versus exploitation, and to the emergence of shared norms, would place the paper in a core organization-theory conversation.

suggestions.direction: Theorize countervailing effects and test them with named moderators. For example, messages may help in ambiguous, low-status or first-time exchanges but backfire when they look scripted or inauthentic, or when the seller's reputation already serves as a formal signal.
suggestions.why: Contingencies grounded in theory (authenticity, the interplay of formal reputation systems and informal communication) turn a single effect into a mechanism-based contribution.

revised_abstract: Bargaining theory treats unverifiable messages as cheap talk, yet negotiators routinely attach words to their offers. We argue that messages work as interpretable claims: their persuasive force depends on whether counterparts read them as legitimate and authentic, and actors must learn which claims resonate. On May 23, 2016, eBay Germany's Best Offer platform let desktop users, but not mobile users, attach messages to offers. Using this natural experiment with difference-in-differences, we find that communication reduces bargaining breakdown, though the effect builds gradually even though users adopted messaging right away. Through planned theory-driven coding of the messages for fairness justifications, relational appeals and identity cues, we will test whether sellers learn from their own experience or by imitating the conventions of experienced peers, and whether the variety of messages narrows over time. We further examine contingencies: whether messages that seem scripted lose their persuasive force, and whether formal reputation signals substitute for informal communication. The study shows how learning shapes the social meaning of claims in market exchange, and how informal communication interacts with formal platform structures.

what_we_value: We value the clean natural experiment and the evidence that firms learn to use communication. But the paper is framed as economics (bargaining under incomplete information, breakdown rates). It doesn't treat sellers as firms making strategic choices, doesn't test hypotheses from strategy theory, and doesn't measure firm-level performance.

suggestions.direction: Treat sellers as firms and test whether communication changes seller-level outcomes such as revenue, sell-through, price realization and growth. Model whether a seller adopts messaging and how intensively it uses it as a strategic choice.
suggestions.why: SMJ needs firm-level performance outcomes and firm decision-makers, not transaction-level breakdown rates alone.

suggestions.direction: Build hypotheses from capability and learning-curve theory. Test contingencies such as seller experience, product heterogeneity, competitive intensity in the category and reputation, and check whether early, experienced adopters gain a lasting advantage.
suggestions.why: Contingent effects grounded in core strategy theory, such as capabilities and the behavioral theory of the firm, are central to SMJ's contribution.

suggestions.direction: Look at the costs and trade-offs of communicating, for example the time spent, lower prices conceded in messages or hits to reputation. Frame the platform's design choice as a complementor-strategy question and set out what it means for sellers and platform managers.
suggestions.why: SMJ expects papers to name the costs of strategic moves and to make explicit contributions to strategy literatures and practice.

revised_abstract: How do firms build the capability to negotiate effectively, and when does that capability pay off? We study small business sellers on eBay Germany's Best Offer platform. On May 23, 2016, the platform introduced free-text messaging for desktop users but not mobile users, which creates a natural experiment. Using difference-in-differences, we document a 14% decrease in bargaining breakdown among compliers. Sellers adopted messaging immediately, but the effect appeared only gradually. Text analysis suggests that repeat sellers learned to communicate over time, and messages that emulate experienced sellers' content are more likely to be accepted. Drawing on capability and organizational learning theory, we plan to test whether communication capability raises seller-level revenue, sell-through and growth. We also plan to test whether these returns depend on seller experience, product heterogeneity and competitive intensity in a category. Finally, we will assess the costs of communicating, including effort and price concessions. The study aims to contribute to research on strategy and capability development in platform ecosystems, and to give sellers and platform designers guidance on when investing in negotiation communication creates value.

what_we_value: We value the clean natural experiment from a platform design change on large-scale bargaining data under incomplete information, with an effect in interpretable units (a 14% drop in breakdown). We would question what economic mechanism explains why cheap talk lowers breakdown, and whether the learning account holds up against other explanations.

suggestions.direction: Write a simple bargaining model with cheap talk (for example, signaling reservation values or outside options, or reducing strategic uncertainty), and use it to derive testable predictions about which listings and price ranges should benefit most. Then test those predictions.
suggestions.why: A formal model that pins down the information-asymmetry channel would turn a platform result into a general economic insight, which is the kind of contribution Management Science rewards.

suggestions.direction: Separate learning from other explanations by using differences in seller experience, the timing of each seller's first message, and within-seller changes in message content and success over time. Also rule out composition shifts in who uses desktop versus mobile.
suggestions.why: Ruling out selection and alternative mechanisms makes the dynamic learning claim credible instead of merely suggestive.

suggestions.direction: Measure welfare and price effects (agreed prices, surplus split, time to agreement, buyer and seller outcomes). Then estimate how much of the remaining gap would close if inexperienced users wrote messages like experienced ones.
suggestions.why: Concrete magnitudes and design implications for platforms (for example, message templates or suggested text) make the managerial relevance clear.

revised_abstract: Bargaining often breaks down when parties have private information. We ask whether allowing cheap-talk communication reduces breakdown, and through which mechanism. We develop a simple bargaining model in which messages can convey information about reservation values. The model predicts where communication should matter most. On May 23, 2016, eBay Germany's Best Offer platform let desktop users, but not mobile users, attach messages to offers. Using this natural experiment in a difference-in-differences design, we document a 14% decrease in breakdown among compliers. Users adopted messaging immediately, but the effect built up over time. Text analysis shows dynamics consistent with repeat players learning to communicate. Messages that resemble those of experienced sellers are more likely to be accepted. We plan to test the model's heterogeneity predictions and to use within-seller variation in timing and experience to separate learning from selection. We will also estimate effects on prices, the split of surplus, and time to agreement, and quantify how much breakdown could be avoided if novices communicated like experts. The results inform how platforms design communication tools for negotiation.

what_we_value: We value that this field experiment uncovers a hidden trade-off in AI advice, where the same tool helps high performers and hurts low performers, and that implementation rather than access appears to drive the gap. As written, though, it reads as an economics-style treatment-effect estimate with a development-policy framing, and it says little about the cognitive or organizational mechanisms behind which advice gets taken up.

suggestions.direction: Present the heterogeneity as a theory of advice-taking and search. Draw on organizational learning and absorptive capacity, plus the limits of local search, to explain why low performers pick or act on generic AI advice that doesn't suit their situation. State the predictions before testing them.
suggestions.why: Organization Science wants a mechanism argued in advance that settles a tension between competing accounts, such as AI as an equalizer versus AI as an amplifier, not a gap in effects found after the fact.

suggestions.direction: Code the advice entrepreneurs implemented along dimensions like exploration vs. exploitation, how far it departs from current practice, and how well it fits local context. Then test whether these dimensions mediate the different outcomes for high and low performers.
suggestions.why: Separating these mechanisms with the experimental data turns a null average effect into evidence on how performance feedback and existing knowledge shape search when advice is plentiful.

suggestions.direction: Theorize what the AI substitutes for and what it complements, such as human mentors, peer networks and community-based judgment, and test as moderators whether entrepreneurs' existing relationships or interpretive frames change how they evaluate and filter AI advice.
suggestions.why: Linking individual decisions to relational and social structures connects the paper to the journal's core conversations about networks and about advice as social meaning-making.

revised_abstract: Generative AI promises to make expert advice cheap and widely available, but theory makes competing predictions. AI may level the field by filling knowledge gaps, or it may widen gaps because using advice depends on the ability to evaluate and adapt it. We draw on organizational learning and search theories to argue that advice helps only when recipients can judge which suggestions fit their situation, a capacity that tracks prior performance. In a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, we randomized access to a GPT-4-powered business assistant. We cannot reject a null average effect on revenues and profits. However, the effect for entrepreneurs who were low performing at baseline is more than 0.20 standard deviations lower than for initial high performers. These differences do not seem to come from the questions entrepreneurs asked or the advice the AI gave, but from which advice they chose to implement. In planned analyses, we code the implemented advice for how exploratory it is, how well it fits local context and how far it departs from current practice, and we examine whether entrepreneurs' advice networks moderate selection. We discuss the implications for theories of advice-taking, search and the organizational consequences of AI.

what_we_value: We value that this is a field experiment run inside real firms. It measures firm-level revenue and profit and shows that baseline capability conditions the result. What we question is the framing: it currently reads as development economics, not strategy, and the implementation mechanism is not tied to strategy theory.

suggestions.direction: Reframe the paper using capabilities and the resource-based view. Treat AI advice as a widely available input whose value depends on complementary absorptive capacity, which only some firms have. Then state contributions to the entrepreneurial strategy literature.
suggestions.why: SMJ needs hypotheses that come from core strategy theory, and this framing turns the heterogeneous effects into a theoretical contribution.

suggestions.direction: Code the advice that entrepreneurs implemented by strategic type: pricing, product scope, marketing or cost cutting. Test whether low performers chose generic or poorly fitting moves while high performers chose moves that fit their context.
suggestions.why: This would turn the implementation mechanism into an account of strategic choice and of fit between strategy and environment.

suggestions.direction: Identify the hidden costs and trade-offs of following AI advice, such as repositioning costs or a convergence that erodes differentiation. Then give managers specific implications.
suggestions.why: SMJ values abstracts that name the unintended penalties of strategic moves and say what managers should do.

revised_abstract: Generative AI makes business advice cheap and widely available. Strategy theory suggests that inputs available to every firm create advantage only when firms have complementary capabilities to select and apply them. We test this idea in a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, randomizing access to a GPT-4-powered AI business assistant. We cannot reject a null average effect on firm revenues and profits. However, the treatment effect for firms that were low performers at baseline is more than 0.20 standard deviations below that for high performers. Low performers did roughly 10% worse, and high performers may have gained over 15%. The divergence does not come from differences in the questions entrepreneurs asked or the advice they received. It comes from which advice they chose to implement. In planned analyses, we will classify implemented actions by strategic domain (pricing, scope, marketing, cost) and assess whether they fit each firm's context, to test whether capability differences lead to poorly fitting strategic moves. We contribute to entrepreneurial strategy and capabilities research by showing that widely available AI may widen performance gaps between firms. We also derive implications for managers and for platforms that design AI advice.

what_we_value: We value the randomized field experiment on real firm revenues and profits, the effect sizes reported in interpretable percentages, and the decision-relevant focus on how entrepreneurs act on AI advice; we would question whether the heterogeneity is pre-specified and robust, and whether the implementation mechanism is identified or only described.

suggestions.direction: Write a simple optimal-choice model of advice adoption in which entrepreneurs with different baseline ability use noisy signals to judge which AI recommendations to act on, and derive testable predictions about selection over advice.
suggestions.why: A crisp economic mechanism, here the ability to screen advice, would turn a heterogeneity result into a general insight about complementarity versus substitution between human skill and AI.

suggestions.direction: Code the implemented advice by its ex-ante quality or risk (for example, expert ratings or matching to benchmark best practices) and test whether low performers systematically pick worse or riskier recommendations, with pre-registration and multiple-testing corrections for the heterogeneity.
suggestions.why: Showing exactly what decision makers choose to do with identical advice, and ruling out alternatives such as differences in questions or exposure, makes the mechanism credible.

suggestions.direction: Design and evaluate a follow-up remedy, such as AI-provided prioritization, curated advice, or human-in-the-loop filtering, randomized within the low-performer group.
suggestions.why: Testing whether a standard remedy closes the gap gives concrete managerial and policy implications for rolling out AI tools in emerging markets.

revised_abstract: Low-cost AI assistance could improve small-firm decisions in emerging markets, but business problems are open-ended, and the gains may depend on owners' ability to judge which advice to follow. We develop a simple model of advice adoption in which AI widens the set of available actions and entrepreneurs vary in how well they screen it. The model predicts gains for high-ability owners and possible losses for low-ability owners. In a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs who were randomly given access to a GPT-4-powered business assistant, we cannot reject a zero average effect on revenues and profits. However, the treatment effect for baseline low performers is over 0.20 standard deviations below that for high performers: low performers did nearly 10% worse, and high performers may have gained over 15%. The questions asked and the advice received do not differ by group. We plan to code the implemented advice by expert-rated quality and risk to test whether selection drives the gap. We also plan a follow-up randomization of AI-curated prioritization for low performers to test whether filtering closes it. We discuss implications for deploying AI to small firms.

what_we_value: We value the firm-level measure of competitive threat, but as it stands this is an economics-style estimate of the "China shock" effect, with a contribution framed around methods and strategy rather than an organizational mechanism explaining how and why incumbents search, learn or redefine themselves.

suggestions.direction: Recast the import shock as a challenge to category or identity: theorize how product-space overlap with Chinese entrants pushes managers toward exploration (distancing, moving into new categories) or exploitation (defending the core). Ground this in optimal distinctiveness and the search literature.
suggestions.why: Organization Science values contributions to core organization-theory conversations, not estimates of an effect for a policy question.

suggestions.direction: Build moderators from named mechanisms, such as organizational slack, status or prior search breadth (behavioral theory of the firm), or how strongly the firm's identity is tied to its core category, and test whether these produce countervailing responses (e.g., rigidity under threat versus exploratory search).
suggestions.why: Theoretically derived contingencies and trade-offs, rather than an average treatment effect, are what make the work organizational.

suggestions.direction: Look at the hidden costs of diversifying under threat. Track whether the new-segment patents get commercialized, whether exploration crowds out depth in the core, and how inventor teams or internal R&D structure change.
suggestions.why: Linking a competitive shock to internal processes and to trade-offs between exploration and exploitation would show a mechanism, not just an outcome.

revised_abstract: How do incumbents search when entrants threaten their market positions? We draw on the behavioral theory of the firm and optimal distinctiveness theory. We argue that product-space crowding by low-cost entrants reads as a threat to a firm's category position, and that this prompts distancing search into new technological and product domains. We also argue that this response depends on slack, the firm's status in its category, and its prior search breadth. Our setting is Chinese entry into U.S. electronic and electrical appliance markets. We measure each incumbent's exposure using text similarity between its product descriptions and those of Chinese importers, and we use a continuous difference-in-differences design. Preliminary analyses suggest that more-exposed incumbents increase quality-weighted and new-product patenting and diversify into new segments. We plan to test the theorized moderators. We will also examine trade-offs: whether exploratory moves crowd out depth in the core technologies, whether they lead to commercialized products, and how inventor-team composition shifts. The study recasts import competition as a categorical threat that triggers distinctiveness-seeking search. It also specifies when such threats produce exploration rather than rigidity.

what_we_value: We value the firm-level, text-based measure of competitive pressure and the link to innovation direction, but as it stands the paper reads like the trade-and-innovation economics literature (an IO-style effect-size estimate). It lacks a core strategy theory, contingencies across firms, and evidence on what the innovation responses mean for firm performance.

suggestions.direction: Anchor the hypotheses in competitive dynamics and the behavioral theory of the firm (performance shortfall, slack, threat-rigidity), and theorize why some firms escape competition through innovation and diversification while others retreat.
suggestions.why: SMJ needs theory from core strategy perspectives, not a replication of the 'trade shocks and innovation' debate in economics.

suggestions.direction: Test contingencies such as pre-shock resources, technological breadth, slack, product-market positioning and capability relatedness that strengthen or weaken the innovation response.
suggestions.why: Showing strategy–environment fit and firm heterogeneity turns an average treatment effect into a strategic insight.

suggestions.direction: Link the innovation and diversification responses to later firm outcomes (sales growth, profitability, market value, survival), and examine the costs and trade-offs of repositioning.
suggestions.why: Firm-level performance consequences and the trade-offs of strategic moves are central to SMJ, and they also support clear advice for managers.

revised_abstract: How do incumbents strategically respond when low-cost foreign rivals enter their product space, and which responses pay off? Drawing on competitive dynamics and the behavioral theory of the firm, we argue that heightened rivalry pushes incumbents to escape competition through innovation and repositioning, but that the strength and value of this response depend on firm resources and capabilities. Using text analysis of product descriptions, we measure each U.S. electronics and electrical appliance firm's similarity to entering Chinese importers. We then estimate a continuous difference-in-differences model around initial Chinese entry. Firms facing greater overlap increase quality-weighted patenting and new-product patents, and they diversify into new technological and business segments. We plan analyses of whether slack, technological breadth and capability relatedness moderate these responses. We also plan to test whether innovation-led repositioning translates into subsequent sales growth, profitability, market value and survival, or instead imposes repositioning costs. The study contributes to research on competitive and corporate strategy by explaining heterogeneous escape-competition strategies. It offers a text-based tool for measuring firm-level rivalry and guidance for managers facing import entry.

what_we_value: We value the large-sample, firm-level design built around a competition shock, and a text-based measure of exposure. We question whether the timing of Chinese importer entry is exogenous, how large the effects are in interpretable units, and whether the measure is validated and general enough to be a reusable tool rather than "methods for strategy scholars."

suggestions.direction: Strengthen identification. Instrument firm-level exposure with Chinese export supply shocks to other high-income countries, or with tariff changes (e.g., PNTR, 2001 WTO accession) interacted with pre-period text similarity. Add event-study pre-trends.
suggestions.why: A continuous DiD that relies on when importers choose to enter is open to selection, and our referees will require a plausibly exogenous shock.

suggestions.direction: Lay out an explicit mechanism, such as escape-competition versus Schumpeterian discouragement, or reallocation toward differentiated niches. Test the heterogeneity it predicts by distance to the technology frontier, financial slack, and initial product overlap. Report effects in interpretable units.
suggestions.why: We publish answers about the trade-offs firms face, with magnitudes (e.g., % change in citation-weighted patents per SD of exposure), not confirmation of a direction.

suggestions.direction: Validate the similarity measure against outcomes such as sales, margins, and product exits, and against existing measures (Hoberg-Phillips, import penetration). Extend it beyond one industry.
suggestions.why: A measure earns a contribution here when it is shown to predict real behavior and to be reusable across settings, not when it is confined to one sector.

revised_abstract: How do incumbent firms adjust their innovation when product-market rivalry intensifies? We build a firm-level measure of competitive exposure from the text similarity between U.S. firms' product descriptions and those of Chinese importers. We validate it against existing industry- and firm-level competition measures and against sales, margins, and product exits. To identify causal effects, we will interact pre-period similarity with plausibly exogenous Chinese supply shocks (China's WTO accession and PNTR tariff changes, instrumented with Chinese exports to other high-income countries). We will estimate event-study specifications that test for pre-trends. Starting in the electronic and electrical appliance industry and extending to other manufacturing sectors, we examine quality-weighted patenting, new-product patents, and diversification into new technology and business segments. We report effects per standard deviation of exposure. Guided by a simple model of escape-competition versus discouragement, we test the heterogeneity it predicts by distance to the technology frontier, financial slack, and initial product overlap. The results aim to clarify when import rivalry spurs or suppresses incumbent innovation, with implications for managers' responses and trade policy.
